analytic.title: ARMS: An Analysis Framework for Mixed Criticality Systems

div.p: The current era of ubiquitous computing and information overload prompts for a collaborative knowledge management and decision support system to pursue genuine scientific research. Diverse results by various research groups in the real-time mixed criticality community mandates an online decision support system to disseminate information. The prevalence of real-time mixed criticality systems in a large number of application domains has given birth to several task models in literature. Rigid certification requirements and accurate schedulability analysis in the mixed criticality domain require appropriate and well-defined task models, tools and techniques. This paper presents our efforts in the design and development of a knowledge management and decision support system ARMS -a cloud-based analysis tool for mixed criticality systems. ARMS is a unique and novel platform that brings synthesized knowledge on contemporary research in mixed criticality systems together and provides a platform to collaborate with like-minded academicians and engineers. The harmonized research results disseminated by ARMS serves both as an exploratory platform as well as a decision support system for assisting industrial deployment. ARMS is hosted on Amazon Amplify and the user interface is implemented using ReactJS. ARMS serves as a ready-made analyzer for researchers to validate their designs and acts as a quintessential reference aid for academicians and engineers in the mixed criticality domain.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Due to significant certifiability issues, the introduction of mixed criticality systems (MCS) to industry is taking longer than expected. To meet the domain requirements of MCS, which must take care of size, weight, power, and certification of these complex systems, new technologies, tools, and models must be designed. Mixed criticality task models should take into account the requirements for certification of safety-critical systems as well as sophisticated scheduling schemes, efficient resource allocation, and system mode transitions. The recent research focus and steadily growing research results in MCS make the practitioner's job harder than before. An appropriate and easy-to-use decision support system based on contemporary research results is essential to evaluate the proficiency and completeness of MCS task models that suit mixed criticality usage scenarios and modeling of apt task parameters.

The goal of this novel work is to provide a thorough research archive and a decision support system to share research in MCS. It intends to offer industry professionals and academicians a venue for collaboration that will increase research results' visibility, producing more dependable and effective MCS. The repository will help in comparing domain needs, task models, and their attributes, and will give a complete overview of the task model parameters that are currently used in the mixed criticality domain.

As part of this work, an ARMS tool for archiving, updating and reporting existing task models in MCS is designed. The associated cloud-based database (DB) gets updated with ongoing task models to keep up with ever-evolving and recent research works. This tool provides academicians and engineers with apt task models required for the domain of study and also provides a holistic view of multiple aspects of MCS. Further, it allows researchers to add and update new task models and schedulers. ARMS works as a simulation tool for task modeling, testing and evaluation of MCS.

Section 2 summarizes MCS task model classification, after analyzing, comparing and tabulating task models with uniform nomenclature suitable for MCS study. Section 3 presents existing literature on pertinent simulation tools. Section 4 provides the ARMS architecture and describes all its modules. It also presents the features and overall design. Section 5 presents an ARMS use case and Section 6 concludes the work.

div.head: II. MCS TASK MODEL CLASSIFICATION
div.p: We have analysed, grouped and attempted to provide a unified landscape of task models applicable to MCS. Our parameter grouping is based on categories such as resources, context switching, quality of service (QoS), energy, fault tolerance and parallel processing. We also have categories based on models that use probabilistic approaches as well as those which use graph theoretic representations.

The basic task model [10], [36] for uni-core/multi-core MCS is defined by five-tuple with elements { ϕ, T, D, L, -→ C } denoted by phase, period, relative deadline, criticality level and worst case execution time (WCET). The WCET is a vector whose size is defined by the number of criticality levels. A task's execution requirements are mapped to the differing behavior of criticalities. This is achieved either by increasing the WCET [10] or by decreasing the period [9] of the task with increase in criticality levels. The variations in computation times and/or periodicity of tasks trigger the concept of mode change in MCS [13]. Mode change influences the QoS of the system. In [8], deadline is represented as a vector having virtual and actual values in each mode of execution. These values are used to ensure the schedulability of a mixed criticality task set. A precise schedulability analysis requires the basic mixed criticality task model to consider practical factors. These factors include shared resources, context switching, energy efficiency, fault tolerance, parallel processing etc. and give rise to additional task parameters. Table I TABLE I: MCS Task Model Parameters These task models consist of non-uniform description and nomenclature of task parameters based on research groups that analyze them, the nature of study involved or usage scenarios applied. These task models require consolidation with a user friendly framework for model aggregation and analysis. This paper presents such an online aggregation and decider framework with a cloud-based DB that has controlled updates at regular intervals.

div.head: III. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Tools help in automating manual tasks hence reducing development costs [43]. Real-time simulation tools for unicore [11], [33], [44] and multi-core [19], [27], [45], [50] systems are well accepted and used in many published works. Most tools exhibit a modular design [11], [19], [27], [33], [44], [45], [50]. These tools provide schedulability and performance evaluation for periodic or mixed task sets. The work in [19] provides a tabulated summary of simulators in the real-time domain by considering features like programming languages used, scheduling profile, design and methodology used and performance evaluation.

Enhanced research interest in MCS has resulted in a tremendous effort towards preparation of tools for certifiability and schedulability analysis. [43] proposed mechanisms and tools to reduce certification/re-certification costs for multi-core mixed criticality applications. [49] presented various challenges in MCS design and development and listed projects that are working to address them. The literature review emphasizes the need for a web based aggregator tool and a decision support system that serves as an analysis and simulation framework in MCS, wherein academicians and engineers can pick and choose the right set of task models for their study and perform the required analysis. To the best of our knowledge this is the first aggregator and decision support system in MCS.

This work proposes ARMS -A cloud-based collaborative decision support system tool for archiving, updating and reporting existing task models in MCS. ARMS is an analysis and simulation tool for task modelling, testing and evaluation of MCS. It provides academicians and engineers appropriate task models based on their domain of study and also provides a comprehensive view of multiple aspects of MCS.

div.head: IV. ARMS: A TASK MODEL GENERATOR AND ANALYZER
div.p: FOR MCS ARMS is a cloud-based client-server decision support system that helps in identifying task models for MCS applications coupled with a detailed analysis. ARMS archives state-ofthe-art task models/parameters and provides a mechanism to choose task parameters, and generate task sets along with appropriate schedulability analysis. The framework also facilitates the addition or enhancement of task models and scheduling algorithms. Regular periodic updates with contributions from academia and industry makes ARMS a powerful and scalable guide for the research community.

div.head: A. Architecture
div.p: The block schematic of ARMS is illustrated in Figure 1. ARMS uses a modular approach. It consists of a server that identifies appropriate task models, task sets and performs Fig. 1: ARMS: System Architecture schedulabilty & experimental analysis and a web client interface/app that is used by the user/admin to interact with the server. This subsection presents the architecture of ARMS and elaborates on the functionalities of each of its modules.

1) Cloud Infrastructure: The cloud platform has an instance of app server, web server and DB server. The app server contains 7 modules namely, Task Model Updater, Task Model Enhancer, Task Model Generator, Task Set Generator, Analyzer, DB Process and Scheduler. The app server modules are executed based on the web server request which in turn comes from the web client/app. The app server connects to the cloud DB for retrieving task models, analyzing results and enhancing the same.

The Task Model Updater module of the app server is used to add new task models by the admin periodically or on user request. Task Model Enhancer enhances existing task models based on new literature updates. The Task Model Generator module selects the most appropriate task model from the DB based on user selection of hardware configuration, functional attributes and usage scenarios. The user is allowed to choose a task model along with appropriate parameters of interest from the list of task models generated by the Task Model Generator. The selected task model along with the chosen task parameters are given as input to the Task Set Generator Module to provide suitable synthetic or benchmark based task sets. Before invoking the Scheduler and Analyzer modules to carry out scheduling and performance analysis, the user is allowed to customize parameters of the generated task sets based on the selection criteria. The scheduling of task sets can be done either using standard in-built scheduler, a customized scheduler or 3 rd party tools based on user selection. The scheduler invokes the analyzer which generates performance metrics such as response time, processor busy/idle time, preemption/context switch/ decision point count, resource metrics, etc. A cloud-based DB is used for archiving task models, synthetic/benchmark task sets and scheduler information to carry out the required analysis.

2) Web Client/App: A web client/app interface is developed to access server functionalities residing over the cloud. The web client/app at the user end consists of a Admin Process, User Process, and a Display Subsystem. The Admin updates/enhances the task models from literature either ondemand or periodically. The update/enhancement results in display of task models, generation of task sets and scheduling analysis. The user requests update/enhancement of task models which will be taken care by the admin after the authenticity check. The user can also propose to add a customized scheduler based on requirement. This customized scheduler has to be approved by the admin to be a part of this users scheduling tool. The will add this scheduler to the DB on a temporary basis by restricting visibility to this user.

The web client/app accepts input from the user. The inputs are: hardware configuration, usage scenarios and functional attributes. The selection available for hardware configuration are uni-core and multi-core architectures. The usage selection scenarios include resource, QoS, energy, fault tolerance, OS overhead etc. Some of the functional attributes available for selection are resource synchronization, message passing, elasticity etc. The app displays task models, synthetic/benchmark task sets and schedulability analysis on the chosen task sets. Results of schedulability analysis are displayed by the output subsystem along with logs. The users' request to incorporate new task models and customized scheduler is submitted through request forms. The admin may accept or reject the request and updates the cloud DB accordingly . The action taken on the request will be informed to the user in a timely manner.

div.head: B. ARMS Features
div.p: The main services provided by ARMS include task model generation, task set generation with selected task parameters, scheduling of task sets using appropriate MCS schedulers and a comprehensive analysis of results. To enable extensibility, ARMS is implemented using a modular software approach. ARMS supports the following features:

• Administered addition/updation/deletion of task models/parameters, usage scenarios and functional attributes from reputed publications in a collaborative manner. • Facility for viewing and selecting task model/parameters based on usage scenarios and functional attributes. • Facility to enable the use of standard/ customized schedulers or 3 rd party plug-ins and perform comparative analysis. 1) Model Updater/Enhancer: ARMS aspires to provide timely and state-of-the-art task model information in the MCS domain. To enable this the admin periodically updates the DB or updates based on user requests. The server services -Model Updater, Model Enhancer and DB process are utilized by the admin for updating/enhancing the DB with new related information from published works. When a new publication or a new task model becomes available, a user can request the admin to add this model. The admin confirms the authenticity of the request by performing the required validations and checks if the task model exists in the DB. If the model exists, the Model Enhancer updates literature corresponding to this model. If not, the new task model and the associated literature is updated in the ARMS DB. Further, the admin solicits the authors to share the codebase. If the authors comply, the code is integrated into the tool. If not, the admin team codes the algorithms and seeks verification from the authors before integrating the code. It is also possible that the authors don't provide the code but provide permission to execute the code by accessing their servers. In this scenario, the admin team integrates appropriate interfaces to access the foreign servers. Lastly, the admin team performs manual experimentation and results of the schedulability analysis and corresponding statistics are stored in the DB. The admin performs task model updates periodically based on the literature review conducted by the admin team.

2) Model Generator & Analyzer: ARMS displays task models based on attributes chosen by the user. One of the displayed task models is selected for detailed analysis. The server services -Model Generator, Task Set Generator, Scheduler, Analyzer and DB Process are used by the user for displaying task models and scheduling/analyzing generated task sets.

A User process can request task models based on chosen attributes and the nature of the study. Task Model Generator service is used for this purpose. The Task Set Generator service is used to choose task parameters for the selected task model and fetch the corresponding task sets. The user also has the option of customizing task parameters. Further, the Scheduler service is invoked to schedule task parameters. The user has the option of using the standard scheduler, a customized scheduler or 3 rd party solutions like Cheddar 3.1 [45]. The scheduler results are used for detailed analysis. The Display Client process provides user-friendly reporting of logs, traces, errors, statistics and scheduler Gantt charts using the analyzer output through the Scheduler service.

div.head: C. ARMS Distribution
div.p: Amazon Amplify (Version 4.43.0), a service offered by Amazon Web Services, hosts ARMS. ReactJS 17.0.1 is utilised to implement the user interface. GraphQL APIs are used to handle interactions with the DB and Amazon DynamoDB is used to manage the DB. Storage is done using an Amazon S3 storage bucket, and restricted access is implemented using Amazon Cognito. Users and administrators can communicate through a web client/app, or web browser. To benefit the MCS research community, ARMS will be made available to users to decide and finalize on the most appropriate task models for their work. Additionally, they will be able to perform schedulability and comparative analysis. At present, the tool is maintained by a group formed by MCS researchers. Controlled access to update/enhance the DB will be provided to users upon on-demand request. The admin team of the working group will play the role of ARMS admin.

div.head: D. ARMS 2.0
div.p: The cloud-based ARMS is designed to work as an analysis framework for task modelling, testing and evaluation of MCS. In this context, it is decided to go beyond the support of uni-core and multi-core processor systems. The first future enhancement is to include multiprocessor multicore systems. Currently, task model/ task sets selection procedures are limited to the retrieval of sample task sets based on the chosen task model and have a limited number of standard schedulers like Earliest Deadline First with Virtual Deadlines (EDF-VD) [8] [15] are in the implementation stage of ARMS. The graph in Figure 2 presents the statistical analysis of ARMS based on the number of scheduling algorithms implemented, research articles reviewed, user logins and number of task models. In future, it is planned to enhance the framework with customization of task parameter values, additional standard scheduling algorithms and the option to include custom schedulers and other 3 rd party tools like profiling tools. Additionally, ARMS will be made available as open source so that users can contribute towards its development and customise it for their own needs, ensuring that it is constantly accessible. This implementation shows usage of the ARMS decision support framework for basic task model with the MCS standard EDF-VD [8] scheduling algorithm. ARMS framework provides a web interface/app that users can navigate to view task models based on user selection criteria. Figure 3(a) displays how a user views task models based on processor configuration and usage scenarios. Both single-core and multi-core CPU combinations are supported in the current version. Basic, energy, fault tolerance, operating system overheads, QoS, and resource usage scenarios are provided for both single-core and multi-core CPU architectures. Parallel processing is an additional usage scenario for multi-core processor models. There are usage scenarios where choosing functional attributes is necessary in order to display task models. For instance, the resource utilisation scenario requires selection of functional attributes such as synchronisation, message forwarding, and shared memory. Depending on the needs of the user, multiple usage scenarios can also be chosen to display task models. As shown in Figure 3(b), the generate option lists the task models in the MCS domain according to the attributes that have been selected. As seen in Figure 3(c), ARMS generates example task sets and displays them as needed. These task sets are used by the scheduler to determine feasibility, and Figure 3(c) depicts this for a hyperperiod. As illustrated in Figure 3(d), the schedule of the task set based on the selected scheduling algorithm is given in tabular form with the start time, end time, and job number. Figure 3(e) illustrates a thorough study with statistics such as the number of preemptions, number of decision points, and the minimum/maximum/average response times for each task. This use-case investigates the applicability of the ARMS framework for the MCS domain and aids in viewing the body of prior research and findings for the fundamental task model. The analysis shows that the research parameters taken into consideration are adequate for system construction and analysis. Additionally, it supports the usefulness of EDF-VD as a protocol for basic MCS schedulability analysis.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper proposed a mixed criticality task model decider tool -ARMS, an aggregator and analyzer for mixed criticality literature, task models and schedulers. ARMS is a collaborative decision support system tool for research dissemination, specifically for the MCS domain. It is observed that such an online cloud-based framework is apt for task model generation, task model selection, schedulability analysis and future research. Regular updates with industrial and academic contributions make this a robust guide for academicians and engineers and facilitates mutual benefits.

A broad range of application domains, including fly-bywire avionics, robotic systems, cyber physical systems, and the internet of things can use this tool. These sectors like MCS have concerns such as the absence of tool interoperability, standard interface definitions, uniform parameter naming, acceptable parameter syntax/semantics, and strict certification requirements. Such comprehensive frameworks are essential in the modern world so that information can be shared to support speedy decision-making. A practical use-case on a collaborative mixed criticality platform illustrates the usefulness of ARMS in research dissemination.

It archives task models based on recent publications of repute. The associated tool assists in deciding on apt task models and generates task sets based on the chosen model. It allows customization of task parameters and schedules them using either a standard scheduler, custom scheduler or 3 rd party plug-in tool. The framework produces analysis results of the schedule as well. To facilitate these functionalities, the admin performs periodic updates and updates based on user requests.
